novedades.texto: Candidate: one previous caesarean with a low transverse scar. Favour success: previous vaginal birth and non-recurrent previous indication. Assess carefully: potentially recurrent previous indication; previous uterine surgery according to myometrial extent. Absolute contraindication: classical or inverted-T scar. Two or more caesareans: planned repeat caesarean per MSPBS Paraguay (vaginal birth is discouraged; uterine rupture ~1.4 %). If she arrives in the second stage: manage as one previous caesarean. International view: ACOG, RCOG and RANZCOG allow vaginal birth after 2 caesareans with senior obstetrician counselling; FIGO is more restrictive. With 3 or more, evidence is very limited. The Calculator estimates the probability of success with the Grobman score. Requirements: immediate surgical availability and informed consent; discuss the risk of uterine rupture (0.5–0.9 %). Misoprostol is contraindicated.

novedades.texto: Group Management Sources 1 Prolonged latent phase and slow but progressive labor are not indications for cesarean. Partograph according to the chosen model (Ministry CLAP from 4 cm, WHO 2020 from 5 cm, ACOG from 6 cm). Active-phase arrest: ≥6 cm with ruptured membranes and no change with ≥4 h of adequate contractions or ≥6 h of oxytocin with inadequate contractions. Second stage: ≥3 h of pushing before diagnosing arrest (longer with epidural, individualized). Continuous support. WHO — Labour Care Guide 2020 · ACOG/SMFM — Safe prevention of the primary cesarean delivery (2014) 2a / 4a Induce only with a clear indication; from 41+0 weeks induction is recommended. Bishop ≤6: cervical ripening (oral misoprostol 25 µg q2h or vaginal 25 µg q6h, balloon, or balloon + oxytocin). Do not diagnose failed induction in the latent phase before ≥24 h of induction and ≥12-18 h of oxytocin after membrane rupture. Never unsupervised; induce where an operating room is available. WHO — Induction of labour at or beyond term (2022) · WHO — Induction of labour (2011) · WHO — Mechanical methods (2022) · ACOG/SMFM — Safe prevention of the primary cesarean delivery (2014) 2b / 4b Verify and document the indication. Without a medical indication, do not schedule before 39 weeks. ACOG CO 765 (2019) · ACOG/SMFM — Safe prevention of the primary cesarean delivery (2014) 3 Same criteria as Group 1 with multiparous standards. Second stage: ≥2 h of pushing. Lowest cesarean rate group: a cesarean here deserves review of the indication. WHO — Labour Care Guide 2020 · ACOG/SMFM — Safe prevention of the primary cesarean delivery (2014) 5.1 VBAC if: low transverse (or low vertical) incision, no previous rupture and no contraindication to vaginal birth. Contraindicated: classical cesarean, T or J incision, previous rupture. Only with 24-h emergency cesarean, blood bank and NICU. Continuous fetal monitoring and one-to-one care (abnormal FHR is the most common sign of rupture). Induction with mechanical methods; misoprostol contraindicated; oxytocin with caution. Epidural not contraindicated. Interval under 18 months: higher risk. EFW >4500 g: cesarean (FIGO). FIGO — VBAC (2025) · ACOG PB 205 (2019) · RCOG GTG 45 · WHO — Induction of labour (2011) 5.2 MSPBS Paraguay: with 2 or more cesareans, planned repeat cesarean from 39 weeks; vaginal birth is discouraged (uterine rupture ~1.4%). If she arrives in the second stage, manage as one previous cesarean. International view: with two cesareans, FIGO generally does not recommend VBAC (only with a previous vaginal birth, senior obstetrician counseling and a high-complexity center); RCOG and ACOG allow it with counseling. Three or more: insufficient data on VBAC (ACOG PB 205); cesarean is usually scheduled. With placenta previa or low anterior placenta, rule out accreta. MSPBS Paraguay — Obstetric conditions · FIGO — VBAC (2025) · ACOG PB 205 (2019) · RCOG GTG 45 6 Offer external cephalic version (ECV) from 36 weeks. Without ECV: planned cesarean from 39 weeks, or vaginal breech birth only with an institutional protocol, trained operator and written consent. In labor: ultrasound (type of breech, head flexion, EFW) and continuous monitoring; inadequate progress → cesarean. Imminent delivery: hands-off assistance. ACOG CO 745 (2018, reaf. 2023) · RCOG GTG 20b 7 Same as Group 6, with ECV from 37 weeks. With one previous low transverse cesarean, ECV may be attempted if she is a good VBAC candidate. ACOG CO 745 (2018, reaf. 2023) · RCOG GTG 20b · FIGO — VBAC (2025) 8 Uncomplicated dichorionic or monochorionic diamniotic twins, >32 weeks, first twin cephalic, no significant discordance: vaginal birth and cesarean are equally safe. First twin non-cephalic: cesarean. Monoamniotic: cesarean (32+0-33+6). Triplets: cesarean. One previous low transverse cesarean does not contraindicate VBAC. Active third stage due to higher hemorrhage risk. NICE NG137 (2019) · ACOG PB 231 (2021) · ACOG/SMFM — Safe prevention of the primary cesarean delivery (2014) · FIGO — VBAC (2025) 9 In labor or with ruptured membranes: cesarean (cord prolapse, uterine rupture). Before labor and without contraindications: ECV from 37 weeks. Ultrasound to rule out a mechanical cause (placenta previa, fibroids, anomalies). With back down, consider a vertical uterine incision. GLOWM · StatPearls — ECV 10 Lung maturation, neuroprotection, tocolysis and PROM according to the preterm labor and PROM cards in this guide. Notify neonatology. Prematurity alone does not determine the mode of birth; it is decided by obstetric conditions. ACOG CO 831 (2021) CaVeSal® proprietary algorithm · Based on: sources listed for each group · PAHO/WHO — Robson Classification (2018). novedades.texto: Placenta accreta spectrum (PAS: accreta/increta/percreta). Main risk factor: prior cesarean plus anterior placenta previa/low-lying placenta. ⚠️ Golden rule: whenever signs of accreta are present, never attempt manual placental removal — leave the placenta in situ and proceed to en bloc hysterectomy, at a Level III-IV center, with a planned cesarean at 34+0-35+6 weeks. Risk factors: number of prior cesareans, prior uterine curettage, prior uterine surgery (myomectomy), history of Asherman syndrome — in addition to placenta previa/low-lying placenta and maternal age >35 or IVF, already recorded under Morphology and History. 2D ultrasound signs: loss of the clear zone, myometrial thinning (<1mm), irregular placental lacunae ("Swiss cheese" appearance), interruption of the bladder-uterine interface, placental bulging toward the bladder, focal exophytic mass. Color Doppler signs: uterovesical and subplacental hypervascularity, bridging vessels, lacunar feeder vessels, parametrial involvement. FIGO Classification (surgical/histopathological confirmation): Grade 1 (Accreta) · Grade 2 (Increta) · Grade 3a (Percreta limited to the uterine serosa) · Grade 3b (Percreta with urinary bladder invasion) · Grade 3c (Percreta with invasion of other pelvic tissues/organs: broad ligament, vaginal wall, pelvic sidewall or any other pelvic organ, with or without bladder invasion). Jauniaux E, et al. FIGO, Int J Gynecol Obstet 2019;146:20-24. ⚠️ Probability and Extent are calculated using the "CaVeSal Classification" — a proprietary scoring scheme developed by the team (not a published FIGO/ISUOG/ACOG score) that combines risk factors + 2D signs + Doppler signs. The FIGO Classification is a separate data point, based on surgical/histopathological confirmation — it does not replace, and should not be confused with, the CaVeSal Classification. Antenatal diagnosis (WAPM/PMF 2026): cesarean scar pregnancy is a potential precursor of PAS — after a previous cesarean, early transvaginal ultrasound to establish the implantation site. In the 2nd-3rd trimester, combined transabdominal and transvaginal ultrasound (placental location, myometrial thickness and contour, uterovesical interface); markers: lacunae, placental bulge, uterovesical hypervascularity and bridging vessels, alone or combined. 2D ultrasound with color Doppler is the mainstay; MRI is complementary (inconclusive ultrasound, non-anterior or non-previa placenta, technical limits). If cesarean scar pregnancy or PAS is suspected: refer to a perinatal center with a multidisciplinary team, blood products, adult and neonatal ICU and complex pelvic surgery; delivery timing is individualized.

novedades.texto: MRS (11 items): somatic, psychological, urogenital. NAMS/Heinemann scheme (total score only): 0-4 mild · 5-8 moderate · ≥9 severe (consider HRT). SOCHEG scheme (broken down by domain, each with its own severe-alteration cutoff): Somatic (items 1-4) ≥8 · Psychological (items 5-8) ≥6 · Urogenital (items 9-11) ≥3 · Total (items 1-11) ≥15. HRT by uterine status: no uterus → estrogen alone. Uterus present, perimenopause → sequential/cyclic. Postmenopause → continuous combined. Transdermal HRT (preferred, especially with hypertension, obesity BMI>30, hypertriglyceridemia, VTE risk): 17β-Estradiol gel 0.75-1.25g/day, or patches 25-50mcg/day. Endometrial protection (intact uterus): Micronized natural progesterone 200mg/day for 10-14 days/month (sequential regimen) or 100mg/day continuous · or Dydrogesterone 10-20mg/day. Tibolone (STEAR): 2.5mg/day PO (or 1.25mg/day in lower body weight or advanced perimenopause) — covers vasomotor symptoms, urogenital atrophy and bone loss prevention (estrogen doses to prevent bone loss and what to do when MHT is stopped: see Osteoporosis and bone densitometry); does not require an added progestogen. Tissue-selective estrogen complex (alternative when avoiding a progestogen is preferred): Conjugated equine estrogens 0.45mg/day + Bazedoxifene 20mg/day — bazedoxifene (a SERM) replaces the progestogen for endometrial protection, without the bleeding or breast tenderness associated with it. Evidence from the SMART-1/SMART-2 trials (12 weeks): significant reduction in hot flush frequency/severity vs. placebo, with a 50% reduction by day 8-10 and a sustained ~90% reduction by day 83 of use; no increased risk of breast cancer, endometrial cancer, VTE, stroke or coronary disease in pooled analyses (follow-up up to 2 years — confidence limited by low event incidence and lack of longer-term data). ⚠️ Availability in Paraguay not confirmed — verify locally before prescribing. Alternative endometrial protection — 52mg LNG-IUD: off-label use alongside systemic estrogen to provide endometrial protection (plus contraception if applicable) — replace at 5 years when used for this purpose (the approved contraceptive lifespan is 8 years, but the evidence supporting endometrial protection in HRT covers up to 5 years). Local availability (Paraguay, confirm against the current pharmacy/distributor): transdermal 17β-estradiol gel/spray (e.g., Ginoderm) — available. 17β-estradiol vaginal ring — not available. Conjugated equine estrogens + bazedoxifene — availability unconfirmed. This information is contextual, to anticipate the availability conversation with the patient — it should not be used to exclude an option from the clinical list. Interaction with GLP-1/GIP agonists: the gastric emptying delay induced by semaglutide/tirzepatide (more pronounced with the latter) may reduce absorption of oral HRT — in patients on GLP-1/GIP therapy, prefer the transdermal route for estrogen therapy (same pharmacokinetic principle as in the Contraception during tirzepatide guide). Order of pharmacologic treatment for vasomotor symptoms (ACP 2026): 1st line — estrogen + progestogen with a uterus, or estrogen alone without a uterus (strong recommendation, high certainty). 2nd line, if contraindicated or not tolerated — SNRI: desvenlafaxine or venlafaxine. 3rd line — SSRI (escitalopram or paroxetine), gabapentin or NK antagonists (fezolinetant or elinzanetant): see Fezolinetant and elinzanetant. Shared decision: benefits, harms, comorbidities, preferences, cost and availability.

novedades.titulo: Fezolinetant and elinzanetant — NK receptor antagonists, non-hormonal therapy for vasomotor symptoms
novedades.fuentes: Pratt MC, et al. Expert Rev Clin Pharmacol 2023;16(5):389-398 · Panay N, et al. Climacteric 2024;27(3):221-235 · ACOG Clinical Practice Guideline No. 13. Obstet Gynecol. 2026;148(5):e345-e364 (Table 2) · Qaseem A, et al. ACP. Ann Intern Med 2026. doi:10.7326/ANNALS-26-01205
novedades.texto: Mechanism: neurokinin receptor antagonists that act on hypothalamic KNDy neurons involved in thermoregulation, with no hormonal action. Fezolinetant: selective NK3 antagonist. Elinzanetant: dual NK1/NK3 antagonist. Fezolinetant: 45mg PO once daily, with or without food. FDA-approved for vasomotor symptoms (VMS). ⚠️ FDA boxed warning: requires baseline liver function testing, repeated monthly during the first 3 months of use, and again at 6 and 9 months. Elinzanetant: 120mg PO once daily. FDA-approved for VMS and also for menopause-related sleep disturbance (a sleep benefit not included in fezolinetant's specific approval). Requires liver function testing before starting and again at 3 months of treatment — a less intensive monitoring cadence than fezolinetant. Indication (both): moderate-to-severe VMS of the climacteric, a non-hormonal alternative when HRT is contraindicated or not the patient's preference (hormone-dependent cancer history, VTE, personal preference). In indirect network comparisons (ACOG CPG13), both drugs show similar efficacy on VMS frequency and severity; elinzanetant showed a greater effect on sleep disturbance (PROMIS sleep disturbance score) in indirect comparison with fezolinetant. Most common adverse effects vs. placebo in the OASIS trials with elinzanetant: headache and fatigue. Place in treatment (ACP 2026): 3rd line (moderate certainty), after HRT and SNRIs (desvenlafaxine or venlafaxine), alongside SSRIs and gabapentin. See MRS Scale and Hormone Replacement Therapy.

Polyps: polypectomy. Severe acute: D&C. Endometrial ablation: alternative, ends fertility. Ablation + LNG-IUS (MIRA2, Lancet 2026): in 715 women under 60 with heavy menstrual bleeding, inserting a 52mg LNG-IUS immediately after ablation reduced hysterectomy at 2 years (4% vs. 10%; RR 0.43), with no more serious adverse events (8% vs. 8%).

novedades.texto: T-Score: normal ≥-1.0 · osteopenia -1.0 to -2.5 · osteoporosis ≤-2.5 · severe +fracture. Z-Score (premenopausal): ≤-2.0 abnormal. FRAX (osteopenia, established postmenopause): treat if major fracture risk ≥20% or hip ≥3%. FRAX and OST are not useful to identify perimenopausal women who will develop osteoporosis. Basic support (all patients): Elemental calcium 1,000-1,500mg/day + Vitamin D3 800-2,000 IU/day (target ≥30ng/mL). Antiresorptives: Alendronate 70mg PO weekly · Risedronate 35mg weekly or 150mg monthly · Zoledronic acid 5mg IV annually · Denosumab 60mg SC every 6 months (do not stop abruptly without transitioning to another antiresorptive, due to rebound vertebral fracture risk). Anabolics (severe osteoporosis/high fracture risk): Teriparatide 20mcg/day SC, maximum 24 months of use. Treatment by risk category (SVGO 2026, Swiss guideline): imminent or very high risk → anabolic first, then antiresorptive consolidation; romosozumab or abaloparatide when the fastest BMD gain is needed, especially at the hip. High risk → bisphosphonates or denosumab first line. Moderate risk → lifestyle + raloxifene or oral bisphosphonate; in selected osteopenia or early osteoporosis, infrequent zoledronate as prevention. Treat-to-target by hip BMD, reassess at 2 years. Check local availability of romosozumab and abaloparatide. Prevention of bone loss in perimenopause and menopause Prevention ≠ treatment: treatment is given to women at high current fracture risk; prevention aims to maintain bone density so that osteoporosis does not develop later. Bone loss is fastest in the year before and the first years after the final menstrual period (≈10% at the spine and ≈9% at the hip at 5 years, almost 1 T-score unit); abrupt estrogen withdrawal (oophorectomy, stopping MHT) accelerates it. Higher risk: the best predictor is bone density on entering perimenopause — with a T-score <−1.0 most women reach osteoporosis (≤−2.5) before age 65. Risk factors for low BMD: weight <57 kg, prolonged amenorrhea after puberty or delayed puberty (Turner syndrome, exercise-related amenorrhea), previous fracture, family history of osteoporosis, illnesses or drugs that harm the skeleton. Densitometry (DXA): in every perimenopausal woman with any of these factors, to identify those with a T-score <−1.0 who benefit most from prevention. Nutrition, supplements and exercise: advisable for all women, but they do not prevent menopause-related bone loss (calcium, vitamin D, vitamin K2, collagen, phytoestrogens and the various exercise regimens at best slow it modestly). Estrogen: oral, transdermal or systemic-dose vaginal MHT prevents bone loss for as long as it is used (also combined with a progestogen or bazedoxifene) and reduces spine and hip fractures by 30–40%. Consider it in women reaching menopause with a T-score <−1.0. Best response in early postmenopause with oral estradiol 2mg or a 0.1mg/day patch; in perimenopause, contraceptives with 20µg ethinyl estradiol are effective. Lower doses protect a smaller proportion of women (the 0.014mg patch was only studied in late postmenopause, ages 60–80). No serum estradiol target has been validated; with transdermal products it can be measured to check absorption. No fixed duration limit; individualize. When estrogen is stopped: the bone benefit is lost within 12 months. Give a bisphosphonate for 2–3 years (alendronate, or one zoledronic acid infusion), then raloxifene or intermittent bisphosphonate to maintain density. If estrogen is contraindicated: approved for prevention are raloxifene (weak effect, does not fully prevent loss) and the bisphosphonates alendronate, ibandronate, risedronate and zoledronate. For prevention, alendronate and zoledronate are used at half the treatment dose: alendronate 35mg PO weekly for 3–5 years, or zoledronic acid 2 doses 2 years apart; then intermittent bisphosphonate. MHT without vasomotor symptoms: The Menopause Society considers it reasonable to prevent bone loss in women at high risk of osteoporosis; the USPSTF (2022) recommends against MHT for the primary prevention of chronic conditions. Use shared decision-making. CaVeSal® own algorithm · Based on: McClung MR, Clark AL. Menopause 2026;33(11):1209-1211 (The Menopause Society) · Bolland MJ, et al. NEJM 2025 · USPSTF 2022.

novedades.texto: Exact HC centile by GA with the Chitty 1994 equation (derived HC): mean = −109.7 + 15.16·GA − 0.002388·GA³; SD = 3.913 + 0.2329·GA (mm, 12–42 wk). Z-score = (HC − mean) / SD for the exact GA. Example at 32+0 wk: mean 297 mm, SD 11.4 mm; −2 SD ≈ 274 mm and −3 SD ≈ 263 mm. Z <−3 SD: microcephaly, guarded prognosis; urgent referral to Fetal Medicine, neurosonography, rule out congenital infection (TORCH, Zika), chromosomal abnormality or genetic cause. Z between −2 and −3 SD: suspected microcephaly; targeted neurosonography, assess proportion with AC and FL, follow-up every 2–4 wk. Most of these fetuses have a normal outcome. Between −2 SD and P5: low HC (borderline); check in 3–4 wk. P3 (Z −1.88) is the neonatal criterion used by the CDC during Zika; it is almost equivalent to −2 SD (P2.3). Prenatal ultrasound uses −2 and −3 SD (ISUOG; WHO 2016). In asymmetric FGR or with uncertain LMP in the 3rd trimester, HC and FL are the most reliable parameters to estimate GA. In the 3rd trimester the LMP is not corrected: it is used as an approximate reference.

novedades.fuentes: Own algorithm CaVeSal® · Based on: Hadlock FP et al. AJR 1983;141:979-984
novedades.texto: FL/AC ratio Interpretation 0.16–0.235 Normal: symmetric growth (Hadlock reference range: 0.20–0.235). >0.235 Disproportionately small AC: suspected late asymmetric FGR. Umbilical and MCA Doppler, biometry every 2 wk; refer if Doppler is abnormal. <0.16 Disproportionately short femur: assess humerus; soft aneuploidy marker if isolated; refer if skeletal dysplasia is suspected.

novedades.fuentes: Based on: ACOG · NICE · Fetal Medicine Barcelona protocol — macrosomia (Sep 2024)
novedades.texto: EFW ≥4,500 g: severe macrosomia; planned caesarean recommended (ACOG/NICE). Shoulder dystocia risk 14–22 %. EFW ≥4,000 g: close surveillance; shoulder dystocia risk 3–4 %. In diabetic women consider caesarean. Ultrasound check at 38–39 wk. EFW 3,800–3,999 g: upper limit; serial biometry, especially in diabetic women.

novedades.fuentes: Own table CaVeSal® · Based on: Figueras F et al. 2008 · Fetal Medicine Barcelona protocol (Nov 2024) · ISUOG Delphi 2020
novedades.texto: Percentile Classification Management <P3 FGR (sole criterion) Refer to Fetal Medicine; urgent full Doppler (UA, MCA, CPR, DV); biometry every 1–2 wk. P3–P10 with abnormal Doppler (UA >P95, CPR <P5, MCA <P5 or mean uterine artery PI >P95) FGR Classify stage I–IV; follow-up every 1–2 wk; delivery according to GA and Doppler. P3–P10 with normal Doppler SGA (healthy small) Biometry every 2–3 wk; delivery ≥40 wk if progress is favourable. P10–P90 AGA Routine follow-up. P90–P96 Borderline LGA Monitor; biometry at 38 wk. ≥P97 Significant LGA Real risk of complications; check at 38–39 wk.

novedades.titulo: Ultrasound category and prior risk (ultrasound only)
novedades.fuentes: CaVeSal® own algorithm · Based on: FMF — Snijders RJM et al. Lancet 1998 · Nicolaides KH et al. Prenat Diagn 1998 · Nicolaides KH. Prenat Diagn 2011 · Cicero S et al. UOG 2004 · Snijders RJM et al. UOG 1999 · Hecht CA, Hook EB. Prenat Diagn 1994
novedades.texto: Category Criterion High NT ≥3.5 mm (99th centile) · or NT ≥95th centile for CRL + 1 abnormal marker · or 2 or more abnormal markers Intermediate NT between the 95th centile and 3.4 mm with normal markers · or normal NT with 1 abnormal marker Low NT below the 95th centile and normal or not assessed markers Markers: absent nasal bone, reversed or absent a-wave in the ductus venosus, tricuspid regurgitation. Frequencies in euploid vs T21: 2.5% vs 60%, 3% vs 66% and 1% vs 55% (Nicolaides 2011). The cut-offs are those of the FMF: NT 95th centile by CRL (2.1 to 2.7 mm; Snijders 1998) and NT ≥3.5 mm (99th centile). The category is not a 1-in-N risk: for the combined risk use FMF-certified software or refer to Fetal Medicine. NT centile: approximate. Up to the 95th centile it is computed with a log-normal curve (median from Nicolaides 1998 and spread derived from the FMF 95th centile); between the 95th centile and 3.5 mm, by linear interpolation. Prior risk: risk of T21, T18 and T13 from maternal age and gestational age only, not adjusted by ultrasound (Hecht and Hook 1994; Snijders 1999). Example: age 35 at 12 weeks, T21 1/249, T18 1/580, T13 1/1826. With a previous trisomy, add 0.75%. Maternal age is not part of the ultrasound category; it is shown separately in the prior risk.

novedades.fuentes: Own algorithm CaVeSal® · Based on: Nicolaides KH. Am J Obstet Gynecol 2005 (FMF)
novedades.texto: High (≥1/100): offer invasive testing (CVS <14 wk / amniocentesis ≥15 wk) and genetic counselling. NIPT can now be offered as a non-invasive alternative. Intermediate (1/101–1/1000): second-stage first-trimester ultrasound (nasal bone, tricuspid regurgitation or ductus venosus Doppler); offer CVS if the adjusted risk reaches 1/100 or more. NIPT is now an alternative. Low (<1/1000): no further testing.

novedades.titulo: Management by risk — Fetal Medicine Barcelona cut-off
novedades.fuentes: Own algorithm CaVeSal® · Based on: Fetal Medicine Barcelona — aneuploidy screening protocol
novedades.texto: Very high (≥1/10): genetic counselling and offer invasive testing with microarray. If the woman prefers, NIPT may be accepted, unless there is an ultrasound anomaly or increased NT. High (1/11–1/250): genetic counselling; NIPT or invasive testing according to informed choice (NIPT carries no miscarriage risk, detects ~99 % of T21, only the chromosomes studied; invasive testing carries a 0.1–0.2 % loss risk and studies all chromosomes). With an ultrasound anomaly or NT >p99: chorionic villus sampling + microarray. Intermediate (1/251–1/1100): report the result and offer NIPT to complete screening. If NIPT is positive, confirm with invasive testing. Low (<1/1100): give the result and explain the limitations of screening.

novedades.fuentes: Own table CaVeSal® · Based on: Fetal Medicine Barcelona · Nicolaides KH 2005 (FMF)
novedades.texto: The Calculator lets you choose the cut-off. By default it uses Fetal Medicine Barcelona; Nicolaides 2005 (FMF) is available as an alternative. Risk Fetal Medicine Barcelona Nicolaides 2005 (FMF) Very high ≥1/10 — High 1/11 – 1/250 ≥1/100 Intermediate 1/251 – 1/1100 1/101 – 1/1000 Low <1/1100 <1/1000

novedades.fuentes: Own table CaVeSal® · Based on: Cicero S et al. (nasal bone) · Kagan KO et al. (TR and DV) · FMF/Nicolaides
novedades.texto: Finding Interpretation and management Absent nasal bone Absent in ~60–70% of T21 and ~1–2% of euploid fetuses; its weight depends on ethnicity, CRL and NT. Integrate with NT and other markers. Ductus venosus with absent or reversed a-wave Marker of aneuploidy and congenital heart disease. Refer to Fetal Medicine, echocardiography. Tricuspid regurgitation Associated with T21 and congenital heart disease. Fetal echocardiography. Choroid plexus cyst(s) Soft marker, more associated with T18 than T21. Isolated with normal screening: low residual risk. 2 or more abnormal findings Increased chromosomal risk: refer to Fetal Medicine for genetic counselling; NIPT or invasive testing (CVS 11–13+6 wk) according to informed choice.

novedades.fuentes: Based on: FMF/Nicolaides — first-trimester megacystis
novedades.texto: 7–14.9 mm: aneuploidy risk ~20–25 % (T13/T18 more than T21): offer karyotype or NIPT. Ultrasound follow-up every 2–4 weeks; spontaneous resolution is common if isolated and euploid. ≥15 mm: low aneuploidy risk if isolated, but ~90 % progressive obstructive uropathy (posterior urethral valves, more frequent in male fetuses). Refer to Fetal Medicine / fetal urology.

novedades.fuentes: Based on: Fetal Medicine Barcelona · FMF
novedades.texto: Positive NIPT: confirm with invasive diagnosis (amniocentesis or CVS), genetic counselling and referral to Fetal Medicine. Negative NIPT: low but not zero residual risk; routine ultrasound follow-up.

novedades.fuentes: Own algorithm CaVeSal® · Based on: Nicolaides KH et al. Prenat Diagn 1998 · Snijders RJM et al. Lancet 1998 (FMF)
novedades.texto: NT is compared with the median and 95th percentile expected for the CRL, calculated as continuous curves between 45 and 84 mm: median from the Nicolaides 1998 equation and 95th percentile from 2.1 to 2.7 mm (Snijders 1998). NT ≥3.5 mm: high risk regardless of age. Increased chromosomal and cardiac risk: refer to Fetal Medicine, CVS or amniocentesis, fetal echocardiography. NT ≥p95 for CRL: increased chromosomal risk; offer NIPT or invasive diagnosis and fetal echocardiography. Maternal age: age ≥35 years used to be a risk criterion. Today the FMF and Fetal Medicine Barcelona use the combined 1-in-N risk, which already includes age; that is why the calculator does not use it as a stand-alone cut-off. Local references: population-specific ranges exist, for example Sharifzadeh 2015 (Iran, single centre), with a lower 95th percentile (1.8–2.35 mm). They are useful for comparison, but the screening standard remains the FMF.

novedades.fuentes: Based on: Gratacós E, Torres X. Fetal Medicine Barcelona protocol 2023 · Arduini D, Rizzo G 1990
novedades.texto: Normal PI: no advanced redistribution. Raised PI: possible advanced cerebral redistribution; correlate with CPR and biophysical profile. Reduced flow: onset of severe redistribution; intensive surveillance, repeat in 24–48 h. Absent diastolic flow: severe haemodynamic compromise; imminent delivery depending on context. Retrograde flow: maximal redistribution with left heart failure; urgent delivery.

novedades.fuentes: Based on: ISUOG Practice Guidelines FGR 2020 · ACOG Practice Bulletin 127 · ACOG 455
novedades.texto: Coordinate with neonatology and refer to a tertiary centre. Timing of delivery depends on GA, biophysical profile and progression. For lung maturation and neuroprotection, see the cards Fetal lung maturation and Fetal neuroprotection with magnesium sulfate.

novedades.fuentes: Based on: Baschat AA. Obstet Gynecol 2011 · TRUFFLE Study Group. UOG 2020
novedades.texto: Increased PI: venous dysfunction. Absent a-wave: severe decompensation. Reversed a-wave: severe decompensation; deliver.

novedades.titulo: UA, MCA and CPR by percentiles
novedades.fuentes: Own algorithm CaVeSal® · Based on: Ciobanu A et al. (FMF) UOG 2019;53:465-472
novedades.texto: Centile by exact GA with own equations fitted to the FMF model (Ciobanu 2019), range 20–42 wk. UA PI >P95: increased placental resistance. MCA PI <P5: cerebral vasodilation. CPR: its percentile by GA is reported with own equations fitted to the FMF model (Ciobanu 2019); the P5 varies with GA (e.g. ≈1.38 at 29–30 weeks and ≈1.44 at 33 weeks). CPR <P5: abnormal; cerebral redistribution, assess haemodynamic FGR. Confirm with a second measurement more than 12 h apart.

novedades.fuentes: Based on: Baschat AA 2011 · ISUOG Practice Guidelines FGR 2020
novedades.texto: Grade Management Absent Preserved fetal cardiac function. Mild Close surveillance; repeat Doppler in 48–72 h; assess DV, CPR and biophysical profile. Moderate Significant cardiac compromise; daily biophysical profile; consider delivery according to GA. Severe Severe cardiac dysfunction: urgent delivery, referral to Fetal Medicine and neonatology.

novedades.fuentes: Based on: Baschat AA 2011 · TRUFFLE 2020
novedades.texto: Mild pulsatility: intensive surveillance; repeat in 24 h; consider delivery according to GA. Overt pulsatility: late fetal decompensation with venous congestion; urgent delivery coordinated with neonatology.

novedades.fuentes: Own algorithm CaVeSal® · Based on: Hadlock FP et al. 1984
novedades.texto: Estimates GA with BPD, HC, AC and FL (Hadlock 1984) and compares the parameters with each other. Difference ≤7 days: concordant biometry, symmetric growth. 8–14 days: moderate discordance; monitor progression. Mean GA: average of the parameters entered. >14 days: significant discordance; the result shows which parameter is ahead or lagging. Head ahead with concordant AC and FL: not an FL/AC asymmetry; correlate with dating, EFW and Doppler. Lagging AC: consider asymmetric FGR (see the Growth tab). Lagging FL: assess humerus. FL, AC and HC are copied automatically to the FL/AC Asymmetry tab.

novedades.fuentes: Based on: Robinson HP, Fleming JE. Br J Obstet Gynaecol 1975
novedades.texto: Robinson and Fleming formula (1975), the FMF standard, for CRL from 10 to 84 mm. With GA by CRL the Calculator corrects the LMP and recalculates the EDD (corrected LMP + 280 days). In the 1st trimester GA by CRL is the most accurate; if it differs from the LMP, ultrasound takes priority.

novedades.fuentes: Own algorithm CaVeSal® · Based on: Snijders RJM, Nicolaides KH. UOG 1994;4:34-48
novedades.texto: GA is estimated with the Snijders and Nicolaides (1994) equation. The rule TCD (mm) ≈ GA (weeks) holds only up to 20–21 wk. TCD is little affected by growth restriction: it helps confirm GA in FGR fetuses. Enter the GA by LMP or early scan to obtain the centile. TCD <5th centile for GA: suspected cerebellar hypoplasia; refer to Fetal Medicine and rule out Dandy-Walker and other CNS malformations. TCD >95th centile: review dating.

novedades.fuentes: Own algorithm CaVeSal® · Based on: Chitty LS, Altman DG. BJOG 2002;109:919-929
novedades.texto: GA is estimated from humerus and femur with the Chitty and Altman (2002) equations. Enter the GA by LMP or early scan to obtain the centile of each bone. Humerus or femur <3rd centile for GA: short long bone; confirm dating, measure the other long bones, look for signs of skeletal dysplasia and refer to Fetal Medicine. The humerus/femur ratio is reported as data, together with the expected value for GA; it does not define a diagnosis on its own.

novedades.fuentes: Own algorithm CaVeSal® · Based on: Hadlock FP et al. AJOG 1985 · Figueras F et al. EJOGRB 2008 · Stirnemann J et al. UOG 2020
novedades.texto: Hadlock 1985: with Figueras, 4-parameter formula (BPD, HC, AC, FL) and, if any value is missing, the 3- or 2-parameter formula; with INTERGROWTH-21st, the 3-parameter formula (HC, AC, FL), the one that standard was built on. Figueras 2008 (Fetal Medicine Barcelona): select fetal sex; if unknown, the average of both sexes is used. Valid 24–42 wk. INTERGROWTH-21st 2020 (Stirnemann 2020): official equations for Hadlock EFW. Valid 18–40 wk (up to 41 if justified). The formula and chart used are shown below the result. EFW Category by absolute weight <1,000 g Extremely low weight 1,000–1,499 g Very low weight <2,500 g Low weight (WHO) 2,500–3,999 g Normal weight ≥4,000 g Macrosomia ≥4,500 g Severe macrosomia

novedades.titulo: Intrahepatic cholestasis: bilirubin and bile acids
novedades.fuentes: Own CaVeSal® table · Based on: MINSAL Chile Perinatal Guide 2015 (icteric/anicteric) · RCOG GTG 43 (2022) (bile acids)
novedades.texto: Form Criterion Birth Anicteric Itching + AST/ALT >40 + normal bilirubin 38 wk Icteric Itching + raised enzymes + bilirubin >1.2 mg/dL 36 wk Bile acids 19–39 µmol/L Mild (diagnosis ≥19) According to clinical form Bile acids 40–99 without jaundice Moderate 38–39 wk Bile acids ≥100 Severe 35–36 wk Bile acids are optional; many centres in the region do not measure them. In all cases: deliver if fetal wellbeing is compromised, regardless of GA.

novedades.fuentes: Own CaVeSal® table · Based on: IADPSG 2010 · WHO 2013 · ADA 2026 (Sections 2 and 15) · ALAD 2016 (Salzberg S et al.) · MSPBS Paraguay · Simmons D et al. NEJM 2023 · Sweeting A et al. MJA 2025
novedades.texto: Before 15 wk MSPBS / IADPSG / WHO 2013 ADA 2026 Fasting <92 Normal → 75 g OGTT at 24–28 wk Normal Fasting 92–109 Gestational diabetes Not diagnostic: repeat at 24–28 wk Fasting 110–125 Gestational diabetes Early abnormal metabolism: high risk, treatment by shared decision HbA1c 5.9–6.4% — Early abnormal metabolism (rec. 2.31b) Fasting ≥126 or HbA1c ≥6.5% Overt diabetes Overt diabetes OGTT 24–28 wk Fasting 1 h 2 h Diagnosis IADPSG / WHO 2013 / ADA 2026 / MSPBS ≥92 ≥180 ≥153 1 value ALAD 2016 100–125 ×2 — ≥140 repeated fasting or 2 h ADA two-step (100 g) ≥95 ≥180 ≥155 (3 h ≥140) ≥2 values The Glucose field in the main form follows the protocol chosen in the module: with ALAD, 100–125 asks for a repeat; with ADA 2 steps, an isolated fasting glucose after 15 weeks is not diagnostic. Between 92 and 109 before 15 weeks, the Calculator shows both readings and leaves management to the physician. TOBOGM (Simmons 2023): benefit of early treatment in the higher band; possible excess SGA when treating the lower band. MSPBS (Paraguay): 2 h 140–152 = high risk of developing diabetes (moderate card). Two-step: the Calculator uses 50 g ≥130; ADA/ACOG accept 130, 135 or 140. ACOG accepts 1 abnormal value and the NDDG thresholds. ADIPS 2025 (Australia): 95 / 191 / 162 mg/dL; reference only. Metformin does not prevent GDM (ADA 2026, meta-analysis of 11 RCTs). Postpartum OGTT at 4–12 weeks.

novedades.fuentes: Own CaVeSal® table · Based on: WHO 2024 (Hb thresholds) · FIGO 2025 (Ubom AE et al.)
novedades.texto: Trimester Anaemia (g/dL) Mild Moderate Severe 1st trimester <11 10–10.9 7–9.9 <7 2nd trimester <10.5 9.5–10.4 7–9.4 <7 3rd trimester <11 10–10.9 7–9.9 <7 The Calculator takes the trimester from the case GA; without GA it uses <11 g/dL. FIGO 2025 proposes <11 g/dL in all trimesters and postpartum, to unify the criterion and prevent postpartum haemorrhage. It is a valid reference; the Calculator uses the WHO 2024 thresholds.

novedades.fuentes: Own CaVeSal® table · Based on: ACOG PB 233 (2021) · WHO 2020 (ferritin) · Holick MF et al. 2011 · IOM 2011 (Ross AC et al.) · Bouillon R 2017 · WHO 2020 (vitamin D) · Demay MB et al. 2024
novedades.texto: Parameter Interpretation Ferritin <30 µg/L: iron deficiency · <15: severe depletion Transferrin saturation <16 %: functional iron deficiency Vitamin D 25-OH (ng/mL) Deficiency Insufficiency Sufficient Endocrine Society 2011 (Holick) <20 20–29 ≥30 IOM 2011 (Ross) <12 at risk of deficiency 12–19 possibly inadequate ≥20 The Endocrine Society 2011 range <20 / 20–29 / ≥30 is the one laboratories report. IOM 2011 sets sufficiency at ≥20 (bone health). Bouillon 2017 compares the societies. 20–29 ng/mL: grey zone; supplement at the physician's discretion. WHO 2020: no routine supplementation in pregnancy; supplement if deficiency is documented or suspected. Endocrine Society 2024: empirical supplementation in pregnancy without testing (trials used 600–5000 IU/day, mean ~2500); it no longer endorses sufficiency cutoffs. Neither recommends routine testing, including for obesity or dark skin. The choice is at the physician's discretion.

novedades.fuentes: Based on: SOAP 2021 (Bauer ME et al.) · ACOG
novedades.texto: <150 ×10³/µL: thrombocytopenia; mild cases are usually gestational. <100: rule out HELLP and preeclampsia. <50: severe; urgent haematology. Neuraxial anaesthesia: possible with ≥70 ×10³/µL if there is no other coagulopathy or rapid fall.

novedades.fuentes: Own CaVeSal® table · Based on: Wiles K et al. 2018 · Abbassi-Ghanavati M et al. 2009 · ACOG PB 222 (2020) · ISSHP
novedades.texto: Parameter Normal in pregnancy Interpretation Creatinine ≤0.87 mg/dL >0.87: outside the pregnancy range · >1.1 (or doubling): preeclampsia severity criterion Uric acid 1T ≤4.2 · 2T ≤4.9 · 3T ≤6.3 mg/dL Complementary; not a diagnostic criterion for preeclampsia Urea BUN 3–13 mg/dL (≈ urea 6–28) Lower in pregnancy than outside it

novedades.fuentes: Table adapted (translated) from Alexander EK et al. ATA 2017 · CaVeSal® suggestion · Based on: ATA 2011 · Endocrine Society 2012 · ETA 2014 · Lazarus JH et al. NEJM 2012 · Casey BM et al. NEJM 2017
novedades.texto: Use the laboratory pregnancy range. If not reported: TSH upper limit 4.0 µIU/mL (ATA 2017; the trimester no longer changes the cutoff). Check anti-TPO if TSH is >2.5 (ATA 2017, rec. 28). Anti-TPO TSH (µIU/mL) Levothyroxine Anti-TPO+ >4.0 (above range) Recommended Anti-TPO+ 2.5–4.0 Consider Anti-TPO− ≥10 Recommended Anti-TPO− 4.0–10 Consider Anti-TPO− <4.0 Do not treat Grey zone (CaVeSal® suggestion): TSH >2.5 in T1 or >3.0 in T2–T3 and ≤4.0: check anti-TPO; if positive, consider levothyroxine. History of the cutoffs: ATA 2011 and Endocrine Society 2012: 2.5 / 3.0 / 3.0 by trimester. ETA 2014: 2.5 / 3.0 / 3.5. ATA 2017 replaced them with the laboratory range or 4.0. Trials: CATS (Lazarus 2012, 21,846 women, treatment at ~13 weeks: IQ at 3 years 99.2 vs 100.0) and Casey (2017, TSH ≥4.0, treatment at ~17 weeks: IQ at 5 years 97 vs 94) showed no neurodevelopmental benefit. The link between high TSH and cognitive deficit is observational. Preconception: treated hypothyroid women, TSH between the lower limit and 2.5. IVF/ICSI with subclinical hypothyroidism: levothyroxine with a TSH goal <2.5 (ATA 2017, rec. 20). Low TSH in T1: may be physiological due to hCG; confirm with free T4 and, if Graves disease is suspected, TRAb. Low free T4 with normal TSH: isolated hypothyroxinemia; not routinely treated. Free T4 varies by method and trimester.

novedades.fuentes: Own table CaVeSal® · Based on: FMF/Nicolaides · Gómez O et al. UOG 2008;32:128-132 · Martin AM et al. UOG 2001;18:583-586 · Poon LC et al. FIGO 2019
novedades.texto: Marker High Moderate Mean uterine artery PI (1st trim.) >95th centile for GA (Gómez 2008); without GA: ≥2.35 — PAPP-A (MoM) <0.3 0.3–0.39 PlGF (MoM) <0.5 0.5–0.69 Free β-hCG (MoM) >3.0 2.5–3.0 MAP in the 1st trimester — >90 mmHg

novedades.titulo: Uterine artery PI in the 2nd trimester
novedades.fuentes: Own algorithm CaVeSal® · Based on: Gómez O et al. UOG 2008;32:128-132
novedades.texto: Enter the GA of the measurement: the Calculator reports the centile of the mean PI and compares it with the 95th centile for that GA. >95th centile for GA: fetal growth surveillance and follow-up Doppler at 28–32 wk. ≤95th centile: normal.

novedades.fuentes: Based on: Poon LC et al. FIGO 2019 · ACOG Practice Bulletin No. 222 (2020)
novedades.texto: Aspirin ~150 mg every night from 11–14+6 wk until 36 wk, delivery or diagnosis of PE (FIGO 2019, regimen preferred by CaVeSal®). Alternative: 81 mg/day from 12–28 wk (ideally before 16) until delivery (ACOG PB 222, 2020). Indications in the Calculator: high risk in first-trimester screening (uterine artery PI, PlGF, combination of markers) and pre-pregnancy obesity.

novedades.fuentes: Own algorithm CaVeSal® · Based on: Gana N et al. UOG 2022;59:731-736 · de Oliveira CA et al. J Ultrasound Med 2013;32:609-616 · Diniz ALD et al. Int J Gynaecol Obstet 2008;100:216-220
novedades.texto: 1st trimester: complementary element of preeclampsia screening. There is no single validated cut-off and it does not indicate aspirin on its own. 2nd/3rd trimester, with established PE/HDP — ≥0.78: suggests severe vascular involvement (PE with severe features). Integrate with BP, laboratory tests, sFlt-1/PlGF and fetal wellbeing. <0.78: does not rule out severity; clinical judgement decides.

novedades.fuentes: Own algorithm CaVeSal® · Based on: FMF · Fetal Medicine Barcelona · FIGO 2019
novedades.texto: 2 or more high markers: high risk of early PE. Prescribe aspirin, serial PlGF and refer to Fetal Medicine. 1 high + 1 moderate: moderate-high risk. Prescribe aspirin and reassess with 2nd-trimester uterine artery PI and sFlt-1/PlGF. 1 high marker: aspirin according to the FMF combined risk; uterine artery PI check in the 2nd trimester. 2 or more moderate: close surveillance, consider aspirin, reassess in the 2nd trimester. 1 moderate: routine follow-up, integrating other clinical factors. All normal: baseline risk.

novedades.fuentes: Based on: FMF · WHO · NICE · ISUOG
novedades.texto: MAP = (SBP + 2 × DBP) / 3. MAP >90 mmHg in the 1st trimester: higher risk of PE; consider aspirin according to the combined risk. MAP ≥105 mmHg: warning sign of gestational hypertension or PE, especially after 20 wk; assess proteinuria, sFlt-1/PlGF and liver and renal function.

novedades.fuentes: Based on: Roche/BRAHMS (sFlt-1/PlGF) · ISSHP · FMF
novedades.texto: Ratio Management ≤38 Rules out PE within the next week (NPV >99 %). Routine follow-up. 38 – 85 (<34 wk) · 38 – 110 (≥34 wk) Grey zone: repeat in 1–2 weeks, daily BP and proteinuria. >85 (<34 wk) · >110 (≥34 wk) High suspicion of PE: proteinuria, liver and renal function; admit if there is maternal or fetal compromise. >655 Imminent PE: urgent admission; individualised delivery according to GA and maternal-fetal condition. Fetal lung maturation and magnesium sulfate: see the cards Fetal lung maturation and Magnesium sulfate.

novedades.fuentes: Based on: ACOG · NICE · PAHO/WHO Robson 2018
novedades.texto: Transverse or oblique lie (absolute indication). EFW ≥4,500 g (ACOG). Classical or inverted-T uterine scar. Breech presentation: caesarean recommended unless external cephalic version is successful (offer ECV from 36–37 wk if not contraindicated). Without a medical indication, planned caesarean is not performed before 39 wk. Short maternal stature with high EFW: suspected cephalopelvic disproportion.

novedades.fuentes: Based on: ACOG Practice Bulletin
novedades.texto: Preterm (<37 wk): assess lung maturation and coordinate with neonatology. Term (37–41+6 wk). Post-term (≥42 wk): increased risk; consider induction and biophysical monitoring. Bishop score: see the Emergencies guide — Mode of delivery.

novedades.fuentes: Own algorithm CaVeSal® · Based on: PAHO/WHO — Robson Classification implementation manual (2018) · FIGO 2025
novedades.texto: During antenatal care the Calculator assigns a probable group with the available data. The definitive group is assigned at admission for birth (WHO). For example, a nulliparous woman at term with a cephalic fetus is placed in group 1 assuming spontaneous onset; if induction is planned she moves to 2a and if caesarean is planned, to 2b. If birth occurs before 37+0 wk, she moves to group 10. Only previous caesareans count: a myomectomy or other uterine surgery without caesarean does not change the group (WHO 2017). The full classification and management by group are in the Emergencies guide: Robson classification and Management by group.

novedades.seccion: Mode of Delivery — Robson, Bishop, Biometry
novedades.fuentes: CaVeSal® proprietary algorithm · Based on: Bishop EH 1964 · NICE NG207 · ACOG CPG No. 9 (2025) · Laughon 2011 (simplified) · StatPearls (CMQCC).
novedades.texto: Score 0-13 Parameter 0 1 2 3 Dilation (cm) 0 1-2 3-4 ≥5 Effacement (%) 0-30 40-50 60-70 ≥80 Fetal station −3 −2 −1, 0 +1, +2 Consistency Firm Medium Soft — Cervical position Posterior Medium Anterior — Cervical score thresholds for “favorable” according to source Source Cutoff NICE >6 Bishop (1964) 9 or more (successful and safe induction) ACOG (2025) No universal cutoff; studies used 3 to 8 CMQCC ≥6 multiparous · ≥8 nulliparous Simplified Bishop score (dilation, effacement, station) >5 CaVeSal® proprietary algorithm · Based on: Bishop EH 1964 · NICE NG207 · ACOG CPG No. 9 (2025) · Laughon 2011 (simplified) · StatPearls (CMQCC). Variant: the modified Bishop score (Calder) replaces effacement with cervical length (cm). Unfavorable cervix → cervical ripening (misoprostol, Foley balloon) before oxytocin. Source: StatPearls — Bishop Score.

novedades.seccion: Mode of Delivery — Robson, Bishop, Biometry
novedades.titulo: Short maternal stature and cephalopelvic disproportion (CPD)
novedades.fuentes: Sources: OPS/OMS Clasificación de Robson (2018) · Bishop 1964 · NICE NG207 · ACOG CPG 9 (2025) · Laughon 2011 · StatPearls Bishop Score · ACOG PB 216 (2020) · RCOG GTG 42 · Consenso Delphi de RCIU · WHO 2018 · MSPBS Paraguay · WHO Robson Platform · FIGO VBAC 2025 · ACOG/SMFM 2014 · WHO Induction 2011/2022 · ACOG CO 745, 765, 831 · ACOG PB 205, 231 · RCOG GTG 45, 20b · NICE NG137.
novedades.texto: Height <145-150 cm is not an indication for cesarean delivery (WHO 2018, FIGO, ACOG): it is a biomechanical risk factor; allow a trial of labor with a strict partograph and, if available, intrapartum ultrasound. MSPBS: height <145 cm → referral to orthopedics and genetics (possible skeletal dysplasia), not a criterion for mode of delivery. CPD is diagnosed intrapartum: adequate uterine activity (3-5/10 min, >2-4 h), dilation ≥5-6 cm, and lack of progress in dilation or descent. Signs: cervical edema, marked caput with overlapping sutures, persistent asynclitism. Once confirmed → cesarean delivery. Estimated fetal weight ≥4000 g + short stature → heightened alert for surveillance of CPD, not automatic cesarean delivery. Sources: WHO Intrapartum care 2018 · MSPBS Manual Nacional Prenatal · ACOG PB 216 · Williams Obstetrics 26.ª ed. (2022) · Caldwell-Moloy 1933 (tipos de pelvis).

Classification at admission and real-time use It is applied to every woman admitted for birth, prospectively: each woman is assigned a group at admission and followed to the outcome (WHO — Robson Platform; WHO implementation manual). Real-time use is institutional: each birth is recorded as it happens to track the cesarean rate by group and plan actions (quality improvement experience). WHO provides a platform where hospitals upload these data (WHO Bulletin). Consensus conference results on contraception in women beyond 40 years of age. Eur J Contracept Reprod Health Care. 2025;30(6):304-318. DOI: 10.1080/13625187.2025.2544754
novedades.texto: What drives the choice: cardiovascular safety (venous and arterial risk) is the first criterion after 40. In perimenopause, menstrual irregularity and heavy bleeding, changes in sexuality and bone loss also weigh in. Fertility declines, but unplanned pregnancy is still possible. Eligibility of each method is always defined with the WHO Medical Eligibility Criteria (MEC). Venous risk (VTE): oestrogen-free methods — etonogestrel implant, LNG-IUS, progestogen-only pill (desogestrel) and drospirenone-only pill — do not increase VTE risk. Among combined methods, those that increase it least are EE/levonorgestrel, EE/norgestimate and those with natural oestrogen (oestradiol, oestradiol valerate). Vaginal ring and patch: conflicting data versus EE/levonorgestrel (Nordic registries suggest higher risk). Estetrol: insufficient data — see Estetrol (E4). Arterial risk (MI and ischaemic stroke): progestogen-only methods, short- or long-acting, do not increase it. ⚠️ EE 30–40 µg with an androgenic progestogen (especially levonorgestrel) increases the risk of MI and ischaemic stroke, in a dose-dependent way. EE 20 µg with drospirenone does not increase it. Combined methods with natural oestrogen did not increase it in post-marketing studies (with few events). Cycle control: with menstrual irregularity, the vaginal ring (EE/etonogestrel) and EE/norgestimate give the best regularity and the least unscheduled bleeding. EE doses ≥30 µg control the cycle better than EE 20 µg or natural oestrogens. Heavy menstrual bleeding, from most to least effective: LNG-IUS 52 mg → oestradiol valerate/dienogest → vaginal ring → combined oral with EE 30–35 µg → progestogen-only or drospirenone-only pill. LNG-IUS and progestogen-only methods can be used with increased cardiovascular risk. Rule out a structural cause first — see AUB — PALM-COEIN. Sexuality: it is multifactorial (biological, psychological, relational and sociocultural), and contraception itself improves it by removing the fear of pregnancy. Prefer natural oestrogens (lower effect on SHBG) or EE 20 µg with an androgenic progestogen. Vaginal ring: possible positive effect (local action). Implant: limited uncontrolled studies suggest a positive effect. Progestogen-only pills: undetermined effect. LNG-IUS: neutral. See also Sexual health in climacteric and postmenopause. Bone: in perimenopause, combined oral contraceptives protect against bone loss. Progestogen-only pills, drospirenone-only pill and implant: neutral effect. LNG-IUS: neutral (one retrospective study suggests fewer fractures). About the consensus: Italian Society of Contraception, systematic review up to October 2024 and vote at a national congress (95–99% agreement on the 7 statements). It does not include medroxyprogesterone acetate or norethisterone, which are not used as contraceptives in Italy.

novedades.texto: TSH in pregnancy (ATA 2017): use the laboratory pregnancy range. If not reported, upper limit 4.0 µIU/mL; the trimester no longer changes the cutoff. Check anti-TPO if TSH is >2.5 (rec. 28). Anti-TPO TSH (µIU/mL) Levothyroxine Positive >4.0 (above range) Recommended Positive 2.5–4.0 Consider Negative ≥10 Recommended Negative 4.0–10 Consider Negative <4.0 Do not treat Grey zone (CaVeSal® suggestion): TSH >2.5 in T1 or >3.0 in T2–T3 and ≤4.0: check anti-TPO; if positive, consider levothyroxine. The 2.5 / 3.0 / 3.0 trimester cutoffs came from ATA 2011 and Endocrine Society 2012 (ETA 2014: 2.5 / 3.0 / 3.5); ATA 2017 replaced them. Trials: CATS (Lazarus 2012; 21,846 women, treatment at ~13 weeks, IQ at 3 years 99.2 vs 100.0) and Casey (2017; TSH ≥4.0, treatment at ~17 weeks, IQ at 5 years 97 vs 94) showed no neurodevelopmental benefit. The link between high TSH and cognitive deficit is observational. Treated hypothyroidism: TSH in the lower half of the range; <2.5 is a reasonable goal. Isolated hypothyroxinemia (low free T4 with normal TSH): not routinely treated. Hyperthyroidism: PTU in T1, methimazole in T2–T3. Never radioactive iodine. In T1 a low TSH may be physiological due to hCG.

novedades.texto: Anti-TPO+ (>34 IU/mL) + TSH above range: Hashimoto's, start levothyroxine. Anti-TPO+ with TSH 2.5–4.0: consider levothyroxine (ATA 2017). Anti-TPO+ with normal TSH: recheck every 4–6 wk (2–5x risk of gestational hypothyroidism). The TABLET trial (2019) showed no benefit of levothyroxine in euthyroid anti-TPO+ women. Preconception (ATA 2017): treated hypothyroid women, adjust to TSH between the lower limit and 2.5. IVF/ICSI with subclinical hypothyroidism: levothyroxine with a TSH goal <2.5 (rec. 20). Confirmed pregnancy on prior treatment: +25–30% starting dose. Neurodevelopment: CATS (2012) and Casey (2017) showed no benefit of treating subclinical hypothyroidism on child IQ.

novedades.texto: The approach to metformin once pregnancy is confirmed depends on why it was prescribed — it is not a single rule: PMOS with ovulation induction/insulin resistance: depending on the clinical context it is continued in early pregnancy or stopped on confirming pregnancy — an individualized, not automatic, decision. Many of these patients reach pregnancy already on metformin and/or myo-inositol as part of their baseline metabolic management (see the PMOS and Myo-inositol guides) — there is no teratogenicity signal for metformin requiring its immediate discontinuation upon confirming pregnancy, unlike GLP-1/GIP analogues (see the Inadvertent pregnancy guide). Prediabetes: individualize according to glycemic control and risk factors. ADA (2026 Standards of Care) does not position metformin as routine in isolated gestational prediabetes — its use follows the same individualization logic as in non-pregnant high-risk patients (elevated BMI, prior GDM, PMOS). NICE (NG3) is somewhat more permissive when risk factors for frank gestational diabetes coexist, where metformin may be anticipated as part of early management if glycemia warrants it — neither guideline indicates it routinely in isolated prediabetes without another risk factor. ADA 2026: metformin does not prevent gestational diabetes (meta-analysis of 11 RCTs). Pregestational diabetes: ADA prioritizes insulin as first-choice treatment (type 1 and, in most cases, type 2) due to metformin's transplacental passage and a preference for more predictable control; it reserves metformin as an adjunct in type 2 diabetes with high insulin resistance/high requirements, not as monotherapy. NICE (NG3) accepts metformin as first-line or adjunctive therapy in pregestational type 2 diabetes, adding insulin if the glycemic target is not reached — a stance more favorable to oral therapy than ADA's. Gestational diabetes: metformin as a second-line agent versus insulin per ADA (insulin as the preferred first line, metformin as an acceptable alternative after discussing transplacental passage with the patient); NICE (NG3) accepts metformin as a reasonable first line before insulin, barring contraindication or lack of response — see also the algorithm already described in the Gestational Diabetes guide. Summary of the ADA vs. NICE divergence: both agree that uncontrolled hyperglycemia, not metformin, is the real teratogen, but they differ in how much weight they give oral metformin versus insulin: ADA tends to favor insulin as first-line therapy in overt diabetes (pregestational and gestational), reserving metformin as an adjunct or an alternative discussed case by case; NICE accepts metformin more broadly as a reasonable first line in several scenarios. Neither guideline diverges on PMOS, where the decision is individualized for reasons unrelated to fetal safety. Key counseling point: the demonstrated teratogen in this context is uncontrolled hyperglycemia — not metformin itself. This should guide the decision not to abruptly stop an antidiabetic agent without an already-defined replacement plan (insulin or another scheme). Offspring follow-up (MiG TOFU): follow-up of the MiG trial children at 2 years (Diabetes Care 2011) and 7-9 years (BMJ Open Diabetes Res Care 2018) assessed body composition and metabolic outcomes after in-utero metformin exposure — with no signal of harm that would contraindicate its use in gestational diabetes; this is the longest-term support available for this specific indication.

novedades.texto: There is no single 25(OH)D threshold. Laboratories usually report the Endocrine Society 2011 criterion; IOM 2011 uses lower cutoffs aimed at bone health (comparison in Bouillon 2017). Criterion Deficiency Insufficiency Sufficient Endocrine Society 2011 (Holick) <20 ng/mL 20–29 ≥30 IOM 2011 (Ross) <12 at risk of deficiency 12–19 possibly inadequate ≥20 20–29 ng/mL: grey zone; supplement at the physician's discretion. WHO 2020: no routine supplementation in pregnancy; supplement if deficiency is documented or suspected. Endocrine Society 2024: empirical supplementation in pregnancy without testing (trials used 600–5000 IU/day, mean ~2500). It advises against routine 25(OH)D testing, including for obesity or dark skin, and no longer endorses sufficiency cutoffs. FLASOG 2026: pregnancy 1000–2000 IU/day, maximum 4000 IU/day. The choice between not supplementing, supplementing without testing, or testing in selected cases is at the physician's discretion.

novedades.texto: Etonogestrel subdermal implant (Implanon/Nexplanon, 1 rod): approved duration of 5 years — already approved by the US FDA (January 2026), UK MHRA (May 2026), ANMAT Argentina (2025 — also covering already-placed implants), and ANVISA Brazil (October 2026 — which also authorized immediate postpartum and post-abortion insertion, 1st and 2nd trimester). Based on trial MK-8415-060 (NCT04626596, Merck/Organon): 0 pregnancies in years 4 and 5, Pearl Index 0.0 (95% CI 0-0.69), no difference by BMI (the trial included BMI 17.2-64.3, 38.1% with BMI ≥30 — the updated label no longer warns of reduced efficacy at high BMI). It does not "run out" at 3 years: etonogestrel release declines slowly (label: ~60-70 mcg/day at weeks 5-6, ~35-45 mcg/day at the end of year 1, ~25-30 mcg/day at the end of year 3), and median serum levels stay above 90 pg/mL — the anovulation threshold — across all BMI categories through year 5 (McNicholas 2017). Independent extended-use studies agree: McNicholas 2015 (CHOICE: 123 users completed year 4 and 34 year 5, 0 pregnancies), McNicholas 2017 (291 users, 444 woman-years, 0 pregnancies; year-4 failure: 0 [97.5% CI 0-1.48], year-5: 0 [0-2.65]) and Ali et al. 2016 (390 women with extended use, 0 pregnancies in years 4 and 5). Dominant mechanism: suppression of ovulation (anovulation) + thickening of cervical mucus. Immediate reversibility upon removal. ⚠️ Paraguay: the current national MSPBS guideline (Manual Nacional de Normas de Planificación Familiar, 3rd ed. 2021) still states 3 years, with earlier replacement if BMI ≥30 — it has not incorporated this update. Until MSPBS updates its guideline, in Paraguay's public sector record the insertion date and explain both criteria to the patient (international regulatory agencies vs. the current national guideline). CaVeSal® own algorithm · Based on: FDA 2026, MHRA 2026, ANMAT 2025, ANVISA 2026, McNicholas 2015 and 2017, Ali 2016, MSPBS 2021. 2-rod levonorgestrel implant (Jadelle/Norplant-2/Sino-Implant): 5 years. Mechanism somewhat different from etonogestrel: endometrial atrophy and the cervical mucus plug predominate over suppression of ovulation (which is more variable with this implant). LNG-IUS (levonorgestrel-releasing intrauterine system) — 3 distinct doses/durations, not a single one: LNG 52mg (Mirena/Liletta/Levosert/Asertia): 8 years. LNG 19.5mg (Kyleena): 5 years. LNG 13.5mg (Jaydess/Skyla — sometimes marketed as a hormonal "Mini IUD", not to be confused with the copper mini-IUD in the following row): 3 years, with lower serum LNG levels and greater preservation of ovulatory cycles than the higher doses. Copper IUD — duration depends on copper load/frame size, not a single value: High-load (TCu380A and equivalents, e.g. Multiload 375, Nova T, Flexi, T Cu 380A): 10-12 years per WHO (the range depends on the specific product). Reduced-frame/"mini" copper IUD (smaller copper surface area, usually reserved for nulliparous patients or small uterine cavities): shorter duration, typically on the order of 5 years — confirm against the specific model/brand's insert, since a lower copper load corresponds to a shorter approved duration. Silver-core IUD (Cu-Ag, e.g. Andalan Silverflex): the silver core slows fragmentation/oxidation of the copper wire inside the uterus — a mechanism that in theory extends the device's useful life relative to a pure copper IUD. However, at least one regional manufacturer labels its "Silver T" presentation with a duration of 5 years, shorter than that of high-load copper IUDs — ⚠️ there is real variability between brands/markets; confirm the duration against the specific brand's insert used in your practice before treating it as a single figure for this guide. Regarding silver's "bactericidal" effect: ionic silver does have well-documented general antibacterial activity in the microbiology/materials literature — but the source educational material (AC Hormonal 2025) specifically describes silver's role in the IUD as slowing copper fragmentation, not as a local anti-infective mechanism aimed at reducing PID; ⚠️ I did not find a gynecology-specific source documenting a clinically relevant bactericidal effect of the silver core on pelvic infection risk — if you have a specific reference for that, happy to add it. All IUDs/IUSs are also useful as post-coital emergency contraception (see following guide). Non-contraceptive benefits of the LNG-IUS: significantly reduces menstrual bleeding (therapeutic use in AUB, see corresponding guide), and offers some relative protection against symptomatic PID compared with the copper IUD. Contraindications (MEC Cat 4): see the WHO Medical Eligibility Criteria guide — distortion of the uterine cavity, active pelvic infection, untreated cervical/endometrial cancer (IUDs in general); active breast cancer (LNG-IUS, due to the hormonal component).

novedades.titulo: MHT and cardiovascular risk — Joint FIGO/WHF position
novedades.fuentes: Benedetto C, Gulati M, Khadilkar SS, et al., on behalf of the World Heart Federation (WHF) and the International Federation of Gynecology and Obstetrics (FIGO). Menopause hormone therapy in women with cardiovascular risk factors or established ischemic heart disease: A joint FIGO and WHF position paper. Int J Gynecol Obstet. 2026. DOI: 10.1002/ijgo.71356
novedades.texto: Window of opportunity: systemic MHT started within 10 years of the FMP or before age 60 keeps the most favorable cardiovascular risk-benefit profile (↓ all-cause mortality, ↓ composite outcome of CV death and non-fatal MI in RCT meta-analyses). Starting it beyond that window should not be considered for a cardioprotective purpose — see also MRS scale and Hormone Replacement Therapy. CV risk stratification before prescribing MHT (symptomatic woman, within 10 years of the FMP): assess family and personal CVD history. Low risk: no restrictions on MHT type, dose or route. High risk: low-dose transdermal estrogen, combined with micronized progesterone or dydrogesterone if the uterus is intact. Intermediate risk (e.g., an estimated 10-year CV event risk of 5-7% on standard calculators such as SCORE2): when feasible, coronary artery calcium score by CT (CAC-CT) — CAC = 0 suggests very low CV risk; CAC ≤10 reclassifies the patient as low risk (no MHT restrictions); CAC >10 confirms high-risk management (transdermal + a safer progestogen). In any category, treat hypertension and other modifiable risk factors before or alongside starting MHT. Established ischemic heart disease: differentiate the subtype before deciding on management. INOCA (ischemia with nonobstructive CAD) and MINOCA (myocardial infarction with nonobstructive CAD): if MHT had already been started within 10 years of the FMP, discontinuing it may be unnecessary. Obstructive coronary disease and SCAD (spontaneous coronary artery dissection): insufficient evidence on MHT use — individualized management, with particular caution in SCAD. Across all 4 categories, if MHT is continued or started: low-dose transdermal estrogen + micronized progesterone or dydrogesterone (intact uterus), concurrent primary and secondary prevention (statins, antihypertensives, antiplatelet therapy as appropriate) and multidisciplinary management (cardiology + gynecology). Progestogen and differentiated thrombotic/cerebrovascular risk: micronized progesterone and dydrogesterone — no significant increase in VTE risk, oral or transdermal (the safer option). ⚠️ Higher VTE risk: oral estrogen of any type, and transdermal estradiol combined with norpregnane/pregnane or nortestosterone derivatives (e.g., medroxyprogesterone acetate, nomegestrol acetate) — the risk increases from the start of treatment. Norethisterone acetate (NETA): uncertain risk, insufficient evidence. ⚠️ Tibolone: not associated with higher VTE risk, but is associated with higher ischemic and hemorrhagic stroke risk — consider especially with a history of stroke or high cerebrovascular risk. Route and dose across scenarios: in any high CV risk scenario, intermediate risk reclassified as high, or established ischemic heart disease, the preferred combination is low-dose transdermal estrogen + micronized progesterone or dydrogesterone (if uterus intact) — consistent with the route/dose already recommended in MRS scale and Hormone Replacement Therapy for hypertension, obesity and VTE risk. Key messages (FIGO/WHF summary): menopause is a critical window for cardiovascular assessment and prevention. Early MHT initiation relieves climacteric symptoms and may be associated with reduced all-cause mortality and reduced composite cardiovascular outcome. Risk stratification is mandatory before prescribing: type, dose and route must be individualized. In high risk, the transdermal + micronized progesterone/dydrogesterone combination is the preferred option. In established ischemic heart disease, MHT may be considered for symptomatic relief after counseling and shared decision-making. Always maintain concurrent primary and secondary prevention (statins, blood pressure control) and use multidisciplinary management for complex cases.

novedades.titulo: Vitamin K2 (MK-7) — Bone and vascular health
novedades.fuentes: Knapen MHJ, Drummen NE, Smit E, Vermeer C, Theuwissen E. Three-year low-dose menaquinone-7 supplementation helps decrease bone loss in healthy postmenopausal women. Osteoporos Int. 2013;24(9):2499-2507 · Vossen LM, de Leeuw PW, Schurgers LJ, et al. Two Years of Menaquinone-7 Supplementation and Coronary Artery Calcification: A Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA Cardiol. 2026 (online Jun 10, 2026). doi:10.1001/jamacardio.2026.1279
novedades.texto: Mechanism: vitamin K2 is a cofactor for the carboxylation of vitamin K-dependent proteins — it activates osteocalcin (calcium binding to bone) and matrix Gla protein/MGP (an inhibitor of soft-tissue calcification, including the arterial wall). Distinct from vitamin K1 (dietary, predominantly hepatic/coagulation-related). Bone (Knapen et al. 2013, RCT, n=244 healthy postmenopausal women, 3 years): MK-7 180mcg/day decreased age-related loss of bone mineral content (BMC) and bone mineral density (BMD) at the lumbar spine and femoral neck (not at total hip), improved femoral neck bone strength indices, and reduced loss of vertebral height in the lower thoracic region. The source consulted does not publish the exact percentage BMD change figures or p-values — refer to the original article for those numbers before citing them with decimal precision. Vascular (Vossen et al., VitaK-CAC, JAMA Cardiology 2026, RCT, n=167 with symptomatic coronary artery disease and coronary calcium 50-400 AU, 2 years): MK-7 360mcg/day modestly slowed progression of coronary calcification (Agatston score) vs. placebo (between-group difference p=0.02), with plasma MK-7 levels in the active arm rising from 0.50 to 6.56mcg/L (p<0.001). ⚠️ The authors and the accompanying editorial describe the effect as "modest" and of still-uncertain clinical significance — they call for larger, longer-follow-up trials before considering it an intervention with impact on hard cardiovascular events. No relevant adverse events were reported. Practical doses (per the evidence cited, two distinct contexts — not interchangeable): bone loss prevention in the climacteric: MK-7 180mcg/day (as an adjunct: supplements slow bone loss modestly but do not prevent menopause-related bone loss — see Prevention in the Osteoporosis guide). Cardiovascular context (established coronary disease): the dose studied was 360mcg/day, in a population with already-diagnosed heart disease — there is no equivalent evidence in general primary prevention. Combination with vitamin D3: both vitamins act on complementary axes of bone metabolism (D3 increases calcium absorption and osteocalcin synthesis; K2 activates/carboxylates it) — see the vitamin D3 dose in the Osteoporosis and bone densitometry guide (above).
